Maladaptive Strategies.value: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I feel on guard even inside my own home
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old woman whose trauma type is stalking, helicopter or aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and maladaptive strategy items all describe hypervigilance, fragmented recall, and interpersonal avoidance consistent with stalking, but no other selected item suggests an aviation-related cue or context. This trigger appears clinically disconnected from the trauma type and from the strong Triggers→Threat / Triggers→Memory pattern in the formulation.

vignette: The sight of a particular jacket or the sound of footsteps too close sent her body into fight-or-flight before her mind could register why — the trigger itself felt like an ambush. That same smell pulled her straight back into the alley where it happened, the memory arriving unbidden and fully formed, as if no time had passed at all. To stop these intrusions, she had learned to keep her body in constant motion, never settling long enough for the memory to catch up with her — pacing, walking, cleaning, anything to stay ahead of the images. The memory left her feeling hunted in her own apartment, the danger feeling as present as it had that night — she could not separate the past from the perceived threat. Already running on threat, she found that ordinary things — a door closing too sharply, a car backfiring — felt like warnings, expanding the list of cues she had to watch for. The checking gave her a temporary sense of control, but by never testing whether the danger had actually passed, she kept her nervous system convinced that the threat was real and ongoing — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off. The persistent sense of danger seemed to keep the memory close to the surface, as if her body was bracing for a repeat and needed to revisit the original to stay one step ahead. By never speaking of it, she had kept the memory sealed and untouched, so that when it did surface it came back as vivid as the first time — the silence had preserved it rather than dissolved it. She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy, and this strategy had become her only reliable shield. Each detour became a reminder in itself, etching the geography of the event deeper into her daily life — the avoidance had drawn a map of the trauma around her.
